Les Noldor entretiennent une relation naturelle avec ce que les Hommes appellent la magie. Pour eux, il s’agit souvent d’une extension du savoir, de la volonté, du chant et de l’artisanat.

Leurs pratiques concernent l’enchantement des objets, les runes, la lumière, la protection, la perception, la connaissance, les éléments, la préservation des lieux et les chants de pouvoir. Ils produisent davantage de praticiens de l’Essence que les autres cultures elfiques, sans exclure la Canalisation ou le Mentalisme.

Les Noldor entretiennent une profonde parenté avec les Sindar, bien que leurs tempéraments et leurs histoires diffèrent. Ils respectent les Nains pour leur talent artisanal et leur connaissance de la pierre, mais leurs rivalités et leur orgueil peuvent provoquer des conflits.

Ils voient souvent les Hommes avec un mélange d’admiration, de compassion et de condescendance. Leur brièveté de vie les attriste, mais leur capacité à changer rapidement le monde les fascine.

Ils haïssent Morgoth, Sauron, les Orcs et les créatures issues de leur corruption. Cette haine est nourrie par des pertes personnelles que même des millénaires ne suffisent pas à effacer.

Professions et formation

La Culture noldorine favorise les combattants, bardes, magiciens, alchimistes, mystiques, érudits, artisans, forgerons, joailliers, architectes, capitaines et diplomates.

Leur formation comprend naturellement les langues, l’histoire, les runes, les arts, la perception, les armes, la magie, la forge, l’artisanat et la connaissance des peuples.

Place dans la création de personnage

La Culture Noldor convient particulièrement à un Elfe issu d’Aman ou de Tirion au Premier Âge, d’une maison noldorine de Beleriand, du Lindon, de l’Eregion, de Fondcombe ou d’une lignée ayant choisi de demeurer en Terre du Milieu.

Elle est disponible durant les quatre Âges, mais devient progressivement plus rare. Aux Troisième et Quatrième Âges, un Noldo est souvent un être ancien, membre d’une petite communauté ou héritier d’une lignée dont beaucoup ont déjà quitté la Terre du Milieu.

Les Noldor incarnent la grandeur et la tragédie des Eldar : créateurs incomparables, guerriers redoutables et gardiens d’un savoir venu de l’Ouest, ils portent aussi la mémoire de leurs serments, de leurs fautes et des royaumes qu’ils n’ont pas su préserver.

  • Sindarin — Parlée 8 / Écrite 6

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

Fëanor and the art of creation

No Noldo better embodies both their greatness and their dangers than Fëanor, maker of the Silmarils. His genius, will, and skill surpassed those of nearly all the other Children of Ilúvatar. Yet his pride, possessiveness, and refusal to relinquish his work led his people into exile, kinslaying, and a hopeless war against Morgoth.

The Noldor do not regard creation as merely a trade. To shape a blade, a gem, a city, or a song is to express a part of oneself within the world. The work thus becomes intimately bound to its maker, which explains the extreme pain caused by its destruction, theft, or desecration.

Kingdoms of Beleriand

During the First Age, the Noldor founded several realms in Beleriand. These kingdoms were at once refuges, centres of learning, and bulwarks against Morgoth. Nearly all were destroyed by war, betrayal, pride, or the power of the Enemy.

The loss of Gondolin, Nargothrond, and the other cities remains engraved in the memory of the survivors. A Noldo of a later Age may personally have known these places, or may have received the tale of their fall from parents who lived there.

After the War of Wrath

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Others remained in Middle-earth, through attachment to their works, love for the lands they had defended, or because they were not yet ready to relinquish their role in the history of the world.

During the Second Age, some settled in Lindon under the authority of Gil-galad. Others founded Eregion, where the Gwaith-i-Mírdain worked alongside the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm. There the Rings of Power were forged, a splendid achievement born from a sincere desire to preserve the beauty of Middle-earth, but corrupted by the counsels of Sauron.

After the destruction of Eregion, the chief Noldorin refuges were Lindon and Rivendell. Their population gradually dwindled as the survivors took ship for Aman.

Temperament

The Noldor are passionate, proud, curious, and intensely determined. They feel joy, anger, love, humiliation, and the desire for vengeance with great depth.

They have difficulty enduring failure, ignorance, or helplessness. Confidence in their own abilities can lead them to disregard warnings, pursue dangerous projects, or believe that no limit should be imposed upon them.

Their pride is not always arrogance, however. It can also take the form of unyielding dignity, refusal to yield before the Shadow, or determination to repair ancient wrongs.

Oaths and loyalty

The Noldor invest spoken words with great force. A solemn oath binds the very identity of the one who swears it. To break it is an almost unbearable disgrace, yet to obey it blindly can lead to terrible deeds.

Oaths may unite a house, seal an alliance, promise vengeance, protect a work, defend a kingdom, or preserve a secret. The history of the Oath of Fëanor remains a warning against words that cannot be taken back.

Religion

The Noldor revere Eru and possess intimate knowledge of the nature of the Valar. Yet they maintain no formal clergy. Their faith is expressed through song, poetry, meditation, artistic creation, and celebration of the works of the world.

They especially honour Varda, whom they call Elentári or Elbereth, the Lady of the Stars. Aulë also holds an important place because of his teaching concerning matter, smithcraft, and creation.

Their relationship with the Valar remains complex. Many feel love and respect toward them, but also shame, distrust, or guilt because of the exile of the Noldor and the wrongs committed during the First Age.

Languages

Quenya is their ancestral language, the tongue of Aman, learned poetry, chronicles, and ceremony. After their return to Middle-earth, they widely adopted Sindarin as their everyday language.

An educated Noldo may also know Telerin, Westron, very rarely Khuzdul, Adûnaic, various Mannish tongues, and ancient or occult languages. Their linguistic mastery is generally exceptional, and they attach great importance to etymology, names, and systems of writing.

Clothing and display

The Noldor appreciate rich, elegant, perfectly crafted clothing. They favour fine fabrics, deep colours, and designs associated with stars, gems, trees, or the emblems of their house.

Deep blue, silver, white, black, dark red, gold, and intense green are common. Their jewellery and ornaments are rarely excessive: even the richest pieces are integrated into a harmonious composition in which every detail has a purpose or meaning.

Weapons and armour

The Noldor rank among the finest smiths and warriors of the Free Peoples. They use longswords, spears, bows, axes, daggers, shields, Elven mail, and finely fitted armour.

Their blades may bear names, inscriptions, and histories of their own. Some were forged in Aman or during the First Age and passed down for thousands of years. They fight with speed, precision, and discipline; their lightness does not prevent them from wearing solid protection.

Magic

The Noldor have a natural relationship with what Men call magic. To them, it is often an extension of knowledge, will, song, and craft.

Their practices concern the enchantment of objects, runes, light, protection, perception, knowledge, the elements, preservation of places, and songs of power. They produce more practitioners of Essence than other Elven cultures, without excluding Channeling or Mentalism.

Relations with other peoples

The Noldor share deep kinship with the Sindar, although their temperaments and histories differ. They respect Dwarves for their craftsmanship and knowledge of stone, but rivalry and pride can provoke conflict.

They often view Men with a mixture of admiration, compassion, and condescension. The brevity of human life saddens them, while humanity's ability to change the world quickly fascinates them.

They hate Morgoth, Sauron, Orcs, and creatures born of their corruption. This hatred is nourished by personal losses that even millennia are insufficient to erase.

Professions and training

Noldorin Culture favours warriors, bards, magicians, alchemists, mystics, scholars, craftsmen, smiths, jewellers, architects, captains, and diplomats.

Their training naturally includes languages, history, runes, the arts, perception, weapons, magic, smithcraft, crafts, and knowledge of peoples.

Fëanor et l’art de créer

Aucun Noldo n’incarne mieux leur grandeur et leurs dangers que Fëanor, créateur des Silmarils. Son génie, sa volonté et son talent dépassaient ceux de presque tous les autres Enfants d’Ilúvatar. Serments et fidélité

Les Noldor donnent une grande force aux paroles prononcées. Un serment solennel engage l’identité même de celui qui le prête. Le rompre est une honte presque insupportable, mais le respecter aveuglément peut conduire à des actes terribles.

Les serments servent à unir une maison, sceller une alliance, promettre une vengeance, protéger une œuvre, défendre un royaume ou préserver un secret. L’histoire du serment de Fëanor demeure un avertissement contre les paroles impossibles à reprendre.

Religion

Les Noldor révèrent Eru et connaissent intimement la nature des Valar. Ils n’entretiennent pourtant pas de clergé formel. Leur foi s’exprime par le chant, la poésie, la méditation, la création artistique et la célébration des œuvres du monde.

Ils honorent particulièrement Varda, qu’ils nomment Elentári ou Elbereth, la Dame des Étoiles. Aulë occupe également une place importante en raison de son enseignement des arts de la matière, de la forge et de la création.

Leur relation avec les Valar reste complexe. Beaucoup éprouvent à leur égard amour et respect, mais aussi honte, défiance ou culpabilité en raison de l’exil des Noldor et des fautes du Premier Âge.

Langues

Le quenya est leur langue ancestrale, langue d’Aman, de la poésie savante, des chroniques et des cérémonies. Après leur retour en Terre du Milieu, ils adoptèrent largement le sindarin comme langue quotidienne.

Un Noldo instruit peut également connaître le telerin, le westron, très rarement le khuzdul, l’adûnaïque, diverses langues humaines et des langues anciennes ou occultes. Leur maîtrise linguistique est généralement exceptionnelle et ils accordent une grande importance à l’étymologie, aux noms et aux systèmes d’écriture.

Vêtements et apparat

Les Noldor apprécient les vêtements riches, élégants et parfaitement façonnés. Ils privilégient les étoffes fines, les couleurs profondes et les motifs liés aux étoiles, aux gemmes, aux arbres ou aux emblèmes de leur maison.

Le bleu profond, l’argent, le blanc, le noir, le rouge sombre, l’or et le vert intense sont fréquents. Leurs bijoux et ornements sont rarement excessifs : même les pièces les plus riches sont intégrées à une composition harmonieuse où chaque détail possède une fonction ou une signification.

Armes et armures

Les Noldor comptent parmi les meilleurs forgerons et guerriers des Peuples Libres. Ils utilisent épées longues, lances, arcs, haches, dagues, boucliers, mailles elfiques et armures finement ajustées.

Leurs lames peuvent porter des noms, des inscriptions et une histoire propre. Certaines furent forgées en Aman ou au Premier Âge et transmises durant des milliers d’années. Ils combattent avec rapidité, précision et discipline ; leur légèreté ne les empêche pas de porter des protections solides.

Magie

Les Noldor entretiennent une relation naturelle avec ce que les Hommes appellent la magie. Pour eux, il s’agit souvent d’une extension du savoir, de la volonté, du chant et de l’artisanat.

Leurs pratiques concernent l’enchantement des objets, les runes, la lumière, la protection, la perception, la connaissance, les éléments, la préservation des lieux et les chants de pouvoir. Ils produisent davantage de praticiens de l’Essence que les autres cultures elfiques, sans exclure la Canalisation ou le Mentalisme.

Relations avec les autres peuples

Les Noldor entretiennent une profonde parenté avec les Sindar, bien que leurs tempéraments et leurs histoires diffèrent. Ils respectent les Nains pour leur talent artisanal et leur connaissance de la pierre, mais leurs rivalités et leur orgueil peuvent provoquer des conflits.

Ils voient souvent les Hommes avec un mélange d’admiration, de compassion et de condescendance. Leur brièveté de vie les attriste, mais leur capacité à changer rapidement le monde les fascine.

Ils haïssent Morgoth, Sauron, les Orcs et les créatures issues de leur corruption. Cette haine est nourrie par des pertes personnelles que même des millénaires ne suffisent pas à effacer.

Leur formation comprend naturellement les langues, l’histoire, les runes, les arts, la perception, les armes, la magie, la forge, l’artisanat et la connaissance des peuples.

Les Noldor ne considèrent pas la création comme un simple métier. Façonner une lame, une gemme, une cité ou un chant consiste à exprimer une part de soi dans le monde. L’œuvre devient alors intimement liée à son créateur, ce qui explique la douleur extrême provoquée par sa destruction, son vol ou sa profanation.

Royaumes de Beleriand

À la fin du Premier Âge, une grande partie des Noldor accepta le pardon des Valar et retourna vers l’Ouest. D’autres demeurèrent en Terre du Milieu, par attachement à leurs œuvres, par amour des terres qu’ils avaient défendues ou parce qu’ils n’étaient pas encore prêts à renoncer à leur rôle dans l’histoire du monde.

Durant le Deuxième Âge, certains s’établirent au Lindon sous l’autorité de Gil-galad. D’autres fondèrent l’Eregion, où les Gwaith-i-Mírdain travaillèrent avec les Nains de Khazad-dûm. C’est là que furent forgés les Anneaux de Pouvoir, œuvre splendide née d’un désir sincère de préserver la beauté de la Terre du Milieu, mais corrompue par les conseils de Sauron.

Après la destruction de l’Eregion, les principaux refuges noldorins furent le Lindon et Fondcombe. Leur population diminua progressivement à mesure que les survivants prenaient la mer vers Aman.

Tempérament

Les Noldor sont passionnés, fiers, curieux et intensément déterminés. Ils ressentent profondément la joie, la colère, l’amour, l’humiliation et le désir de vengeance.

Ils supportent difficilement l’échec, l’ignorance ou l’impuissance. Leur confiance en leurs capacités peut les conduire à sous-estimer les avertissements, à poursuivre un projet dangereux ou à croire qu’aucune limite ne saurait leur être imposée.

Leur orgueil n’est cependant pas toujours de l’arrogance. Il peut aussi prendre la forme d’une dignité inflexible, d’un refus de céder devant l’Ombre ou d’une volonté de réparer les fautes anciennes.

Serments et fidélité

Les Noldor donnent une grande force aux paroles prononcées. Un serment solennel engage l’identité même de celui qui le prête. Le rompre est une honte presque insupportable, mais le respecter aveuglément peut conduire à des actes terribles.

Les serments servent à unir une maison, sceller une alliance, promettre une vengeance, protéger une œuvre, défendre un royaume ou préserver un secret. L’histoire du serment de Fëanor demeure un avertissement contre les paroles impossibles à reprendre.

Religion

Les Noldor révèrent Eru et connaissent intimement la nature des Valar. Ils n’entretiennent pourtant pas de clergé formel. Leur foi s’exprime par le chant, la poésie, la méditation, la création artistique et la célébration des œuvres du monde.

Ils honorent particulièrement Varda, qu’ils nomment Elentári ou Elbereth, la Dame des Étoiles. Aulë occupe également une place importante en raison de son enseignement des arts de la matière, de la forge et de la création.

Leur relation avec les Valar reste complexe. Beaucoup éprouvent à leur égard amour et respect, mais aussi honte, défiance ou culpabilité en raison de l’exil des Noldor et des fautes du Premier Âge.

Langues

Le quenya est leur langue ancestrale, langue d’Aman, de la poésie savante, des chroniques et des cérémonies. Après leur retour en Terre du Milieu, ils adoptèrent largement le sindarin comme langue quotidienne.

Un Noldo instruit peut également connaître le telerin, le westron, très rarement le khuzdul, l’adûnaïque, diverses langues humaines et des langues anciennes ou occultes. Leur maîtrise linguistique est généralement exceptionnelle et ils accordent une grande importance à l’étymologie, aux noms et aux systèmes d’écriture.

Vêtements et apparat

Les Noldor apprécient les vêtements riches, élégants et parfaitement façonnés. Ils privilégient les étoffes fines, les couleurs profondes et les motifs liés aux étoiles, aux gemmes, aux arbres ou aux emblèmes de leur maison.

Le bleu profond, l’argent, le blanc, le noir, le rouge sombre, l’or et le vert intense sont fréquents. Leurs bijoux et ornements sont rarement excessifs : même les pièces les plus riches sont intégrées à une composition harmonieuse où chaque détail possède une fonction ou une signification.

Armes et armures

Les Noldor comptent parmi les meilleurs forgerons et guerriers des Peuples Libres. Ils utilisent épées longues, lances, arcs, haches, dagues, boucliers, mailles elfiques et armures finement ajustées.

Leurs lames peuvent porter des noms, des inscriptions et une histoire propre. Certaines furent forgées en Aman ou au Premier Âge et transmises durant des milliers d’années. Ils combattent avec rapidité, précision et discipline ; leur légèreté ne les empêche pas de porter des protections solides.

Magie

Les Noldor entretiennent une relation naturelle avec ce que les Hommes appellent la magie. Pour eux, il s’agit souvent d’une extension du savoir, de la volonté, du chant et de l’artisanat.

Leurs pratiques concernent l’enchantement des objets, les runes, la lumière, la protection, la perception, la connaissance, les éléments, la préservation des lieux et les chants de pouvoir. Ils produisent davantage de praticiens de l’Essence que les autres cultures elfiques, sans exclure la Canalisation ou le Mentalisme.

Relations avec les autres peuples

Les Noldor entretiennent une profonde parenté avec les Sindar, bien que leurs tempéraments et leurs histoires diffèrent. Ils respectent les Nains pour leur talent artisanal et leur connaissance de la pierre, mais leurs rivalités et leur orgueil peuvent provoquer des conflits.

Ils voient souvent les Hommes avec un mélange d’admiration, de compassion et de condescendance. Leur brièveté de vie les attriste, mais leur capacité à changer rapidement le monde les fascine.

Ils haïssent Morgoth, Sauron, les Orcs et les créatures issues de leur corruption. Cette haine est nourrie par des pertes personnelles que même des millénaires ne suffisent pas à effacer.

Professions et formation

La Culture noldorine favorise les combattants, bardes, magiciens, alchimistes, mystiques, érudits, artisans, forgerons, joailliers, architectes, capitaines et diplomates.

Leur formation comprend naturellement les langues, l’histoire, les runes, les arts, la perception, les armes, la magie, la forge, l’artisanat et la connaissance des peuples.

Place dans la création de personnage

Elle est disponible durant les quatre Âges, mais devient progressivement plus rare. Aux Troisième et Quatrième Âges, un Noldo est souvent un être ancien, membre d’une petite communauté ou héritier d’une lignée dont beaucoup ont déjà quitté la Terre du Milieu.

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

Fëanor and the art of creation

No Noldo better embodies both their greatness and their dangers than Fëanor, maker of the Silmarils. His genius, will, and skill surpassed those of nearly all the other Children of Ilúvatar. Yet his pride, possessiveness, and refusal to relinquish his work led his people into exile, kinslaying, and a hopeless war against Morgoth.

The Noldor do not regard creation as merely a trade. To shape a blade, a gem, a city, or a song is to express a part of oneself within the world. The work thus becomes intimately bound to its maker, which explains the extreme pain caused by its destruction, theft, or desecration.

Kingdoms of Beleriand

During the First Age, the Noldor founded several realms in Beleriand. These kingdoms were at once refuges, centres of learning, and bulwarks against Morgoth. Nearly all were destroyed by war, betrayal, pride, or the power of the Enemy.

The loss of Gondolin, Nargothrond, and the other cities remains engraved in the memory of the survivors. A Noldo of a later Age may personally have known these places, or may have received the tale of their fall from parents who lived there.

After the War of Wrath

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Others remained in Middle-earth, through attachment to their works, love for the lands they had defended, or because they were not yet ready to relinquish their role in the history of the world.

During the Second Age, some settled in Lindon under the authority of Gil-galad. Others founded Eregion, where the Gwaith-i-Mírdain worked alongside the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm. There the Rings of Power were forged, a splendid achievement born from a sincere desire to preserve the beauty of Middle-earth, but corrupted by the counsels of Sauron.

After the destruction of Eregion, the chief Noldorin refuges were Lindon and Rivendell. Their population gradually dwindled as the survivors took ship for Aman.

Temperament

The Noldor are passionate, proud, curious, and intensely determined. They feel joy, anger, love, humiliation, and the desire for vengeance with great depth.

They have difficulty enduring failure, ignorance, or helplessness. Confidence in their own abilities can lead them to disregard warnings, pursue dangerous projects, or believe that no limit should be imposed upon them.

Their pride is not always arrogance, however. It can also take the form of unyielding dignity, refusal to yield before the Shadow, or determination to repair ancient wrongs.

Oaths and loyalty

The Noldor invest spoken words with great force. A solemn oath binds the very identity of the one who swears it. To break it is an almost unbearable disgrace, yet to obey it blindly can lead to terrible deeds.

Oaths may unite a house, seal an alliance, promise vengeance, protect a work, defend a kingdom, or preserve a secret. The history of the Oath of Fëanor remains a warning against words that cannot be taken back.

Religion

The Noldor revere Eru and possess intimate knowledge of the nature of the Valar. Yet they maintain no formal clergy. Their faith is expressed through song, poetry, meditation, artistic creation, and celebration of the works of the world.

They especially honour Varda, whom they call Elentári or Elbereth, the Lady of the Stars. Aulë also holds an important place because of his teaching concerning matter, smithcraft, and creation.

Their relationship with the Valar remains complex. Many feel love and respect toward them, but also shame, distrust, or guilt because of the exile of the Noldor and the wrongs committed during the First Age.

Languages

Quenya is their ancestral language, the tongue of Aman, learned poetry, chronicles, and ceremony. After their return to Middle-earth, they widely adopted Sindarin as their everyday language.

An educated Noldo may also know Telerin, Westron, very rarely Khuzdul, Adûnaic, various Mannish tongues, and ancient or occult languages. Their linguistic mastery is generally exceptional, and they attach great importance to etymology, names, and systems of writing.

Clothing and display

The Noldor appreciate rich, elegant, perfectly crafted clothing. They favour fine fabrics, deep colours, and designs associated with stars, gems, trees, or the emblems of their house.

Deep blue, silver, white, black, dark red, gold, and intense green are common. Their jewellery and ornaments are rarely excessive: even the richest pieces are integrated into a harmonious composition in which every detail has a purpose or meaning.

Weapons and armour

The Noldor rank among the finest smiths and warriors of the Free Peoples. They use longswords, spears, bows, axes, daggers, shields, Elven mail, and finely fitted armour.

Their blades may bear names, inscriptions, and histories of their own. Some were forged in Aman or during the First Age and passed down for thousands of years. They fight with speed, precision, and discipline; their lightness does not prevent them from wearing solid protection.

Magic

The Noldor have a natural relationship with what Men call magic. To them, it is often an extension of knowledge, will, song, and craft.

Their practices concern the enchantment of objects, runes, light, protection, perception, knowledge, the elements, preservation of places, and songs of power. They produce more practitioners of Essence than other Elven cultures, without excluding Channeling or Mentalism.

Relations with other peoples

The Noldor share deep kinship with the Sindar, although their temperaments and histories differ. They respect Dwarves for their craftsmanship and knowledge of stone, but rivalry and pride can provoke conflict.

They often view Men with a mixture of admiration, compassion, and condescension. The brevity of human life saddens them, while humanity's ability to change the world quickly fascinates them.

They hate Morgoth, Sauron, Orcs, and creatures born of their corruption. This hatred is nourished by personal losses that even millennia are insufficient to erase.

Professions and training

Noldorin Culture favours warriors, bards, magicians, alchemists, mystics, scholars, craftsmen, smiths, jewellers, architects, captains, and diplomats.

Their training naturally includes languages, history, runes, the arts, perception, weapons, magic, smithcraft, crafts, and knowledge of peoples.

Place in character creation

Noldorin Culture is particularly appropriate for an Elf from Aman or Tirion in the First Age, a Noldorin house of Beleriand, Lindon, Eregion, Rivendell, or a lineage that chose to remain in Middle-earth.

It is available during all four Ages, but becomes progressively rarer. In the Third and Fourth Ages, a Noldo is often an ancient being, a member of a small community, or the heir of a lineage many of whose members have already left Middle-earth.

The Noldor embody both the grandeur and tragedy of the Eldar: incomparable creators, formidable warriors, and guardians of lore brought from the West, they also bear the memory of their oaths, their faults, and the kingdoms they failed to preserve.

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Oaths and loyalty

The Noldor invest spoken words with great force. A solemn oath binds the very identity of the one who swears it. To break it is an almost unbearable disgrace, yet to obey it blindly can lead to terrible deeds.

Oaths may unite a house, seal an alliance, promise vengeance, protect a work, defend a kingdom, or preserve a secret. The history of the Oath of Fëanor remains a warning against words that cannot be taken back.

Religion

The Noldor revere Eru and possess intimate knowledge of the nature of the Valar. Yet they maintain no formal clergy. Their faith is expressed through song, poetry, meditation, artistic creation, and celebration of the works of the world.

They especially honour Varda, whom they call Elentári or Elbereth, the Lady of the Stars. Aulë also holds an important place because of his teaching concerning matter, smithcraft, and creation.

Their relationship with the Valar remains complex. Many feel love and respect toward them, but also shame, distrust, or guilt because of the exile of the Noldor and the wrongs committed during the First Age.

Languages

Quenya is their ancestral language, the tongue of Aman, learned poetry, chronicles, and ceremony. After their return to Middle-earth, they widely adopted Sindarin as their everyday language.

An educated Noldo may also know Telerin, Westron, very rarely Khuzdul, Adûnaic, various Mannish tongues, and ancient or occult languages. Their linguistic mastery is generally exceptional, and they attach great importance to etymology, names, and systems of writing.

Clothing and display

The Noldor appreciate rich, elegant, perfectly crafted clothing. They favour fine fabrics, deep colours, and designs associated with stars, gems, trees, or the emblems of their house.

Deep blue, silver, white, black, dark red, gold, and intense green are common. Their jewellery and ornaments are rarely excessive: even the richest pieces are integrated into a harmonious composition in which every detail has a purpose or meaning.

Weapons and armour

The Noldor rank among the finest smiths and warriors of the Free Peoples. They use longswords, spears, bows, axes, daggers, shields, Elven mail, and finely fitted armour.

Their blades may bear names, inscriptions, and histories of their own. Some were forged in Aman or during the First Age and passed down for thousands of years. They fight with speed, precision, and discipline; their lightness does not prevent them from wearing solid protection.

Magic

The Noldor have a natural relationship with what Men call magic. To them, it is often an extension of knowledge, will, song, and craft.

Their practices concern the enchantment of objects, runes, light, protection, perception, knowledge, the elements, preservation of places, and songs of power. They produce more practitioners of Essence than other Elven cultures, without excluding Channeling or Mentalism.

Relations with other peoples

The Noldor share deep kinship with the Sindar, although their temperaments and histories differ. They respect Dwarves for their craftsmanship and knowledge of stone, but rivalry and pride can provoke conflict.

They often view Men with a mixture of admiration, compassion, and condescension. The brevity of human life saddens them, while humanity's ability to change the world quickly fascinates them.

They hate Morgoth, Sauron, Orcs, and creatures born of their corruption. This hatred is nourished by personal losses that even millennia are insufficient to erase.

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

Fëanor and the art of creation

No Noldo better embodies both their greatness and their dangers than Fëanor, maker of the Silmarils. His genius, will, and skill surpassed those of nearly all the other Children of Ilúvatar. Yet his pride, possessiveness, and refusal to relinquish his work led his people into exile, kinslaying, and a hopeless war against Morgoth.

The Noldor do not regard creation as merely a trade. To shape a blade, a gem, a city, or a song is to express a part of oneself within the world. The work thus becomes intimately bound to its maker, which explains the extreme pain caused by its destruction, theft, or desecration.

Kingdoms of Beleriand

During the First Age, the Noldor founded several realms in Beleriand. These kingdoms were at once refuges, centres of learning, and bulwarks against Morgoth. Nearly all were destroyed by war, betrayal, pride, or the power of the Enemy.

The loss of Gondolin, Nargothrond, and the other cities remains engraved in the memory of the survivors. A Noldo of a later Age may personally have known these places, or may have received the tale of their fall from parents who lived there.

After the War of Wrath

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Others remained in Middle-earth, through attachment to their works, love for the lands they had defended, or because they were not yet ready to relinquish their role in the history of the world.

During the Second Age, some settled in Lindon under the authority of Gil-galad. Others founded Eregion, where the Gwaith-i-Mírdain worked alongside the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm. There the Rings of Power were forged, a splendid achievement born from a sincere desire to preserve the beauty of Middle-earth, but corrupted by the counsels of Sauron.

After the destruction of Eregion, the chief Noldorin refuges were Lindon and Rivendell. Their population gradually dwindled as the survivors took ship for Aman.

Temperament

The Noldor are passionate, proud, curious, and intensely determined. They feel joy, anger, love, humiliation, and the desire for vengeance with great depth.

They have difficulty enduring failure, ignorance, or helplessness. Confidence in their own abilities can lead them to disregard warnings, pursue dangerous projects, or believe that no limit should be imposed upon them.

Their pride is not always arrogance, however. It can also take the form of unyielding dignity, refusal to yield before the Shadow, or determination to repair ancient wrongs.

Oaths and loyalty

The Noldor invest spoken words with great force. A solemn oath binds the very identity of the one who swears it. To break it is an almost unbearable disgrace, yet to obey it blindly can lead to terrible deeds.

Oaths may unite a house, seal an alliance, promise vengeance, protect a work, defend a kingdom, or preserve a secret. The history of the Oath of Fëanor remains a warning against words that cannot be taken back.

Religion

The Noldor revere Eru and possess intimate knowledge of the nature of the Valar. Yet they maintain no formal clergy. Their faith is expressed through song, poetry, meditation, artistic creation, and celebration of the works of the world.

They especially honour Varda, whom they call Elentári or Elbereth, the Lady of the Stars. Aulë also holds an important place because of his teaching concerning matter, smithcraft, and creation.

Their relationship with the Valar remains complex. Many feel love and respect toward them, but also shame, distrust, or guilt because of the exile of the Noldor and the wrongs committed during the First Age.

Languages

Quenya is their ancestral language, the tongue of Aman, learned poetry, chronicles, and ceremony. After their return to Middle-earth, they widely adopted Sindarin as their everyday language.

An educated Noldo may also know Telerin, Westron, very rarely Khuzdul, Adûnaic, various Mannish tongues, and ancient or occult languages. Their linguistic mastery is generally exceptional, and they attach great importance to etymology, names, and systems of writing.

Clothing and display

The Noldor appreciate rich, elegant, perfectly crafted clothing. They favour fine fabrics, deep colours, and designs associated with stars, gems, trees, or the emblems of their house.

Deep blue, silver, white, black, dark red, gold, and intense green are common. Their jewellery and ornaments are rarely excessive: even the richest pieces are integrated into a harmonious composition in which every detail has a purpose or meaning.

Weapons and armour

The Noldor rank among the finest smiths and warriors of the Free Peoples. They use longswords, spears, bows, axes, daggers, shields, Elven mail, and finely fitted armour.

Their blades may bear names, inscriptions, and histories of their own. Some were forged in Aman or during the First Age and passed down for thousands of years. They fight with speed, precision, and discipline; their lightness does not prevent them from wearing solid protection.

Magic

The Noldor have a natural relationship with what Men call magic. To them, it is often an extension of knowledge, will, song, and craft.

Their practices concern the enchantment of objects, runes, light, protection, perception, knowledge, the elements, preservation of places, and songs of power. They produce more practitioners of Essence than other Elven cultures, without excluding Channeling or Mentalism.

Relations with other peoples

The Noldor share deep kinship with the Sindar, although their temperaments and histories differ. They respect Dwarves for their craftsmanship and knowledge of stone, but rivalry and pride can provoke conflict.

They often view Men with a mixture of admiration, compassion, and condescension. The brevity of human life saddens them, while humanity's ability to change the world quickly fascinates them.

They hate Morgoth, Sauron, Orcs, and creatures born of their corruption. This hatred is nourished by personal losses that even millennia are insufficient to erase.

Professions and training

Noldorin Culture favours warriors, bards, magicians, alchemists, mystics, scholars, craftsmen, smiths, jewellers, architects, captains, and diplomats.

Their training naturally includes languages, history, runes, the arts, perception, weapons, magic, smithcraft, crafts, and knowledge of peoples.

Place in character creation

Noldorin Culture is particularly appropriate for an Elf from Aman or Tirion in the First Age, a Noldorin house of Beleriand, Lindon, Eregion, Rivendell, or a lineage that chose to remain in Middle-earth.

It is available during all four Ages, but becomes progressively rarer. In the Third and Fourth Ages, a Noldo is often an ancient being, a member of a small community, or the heir of a lineage many of whose members have already left Middle-earth.

The Noldor embody both the grandeur and tragedy of the Eldar: incomparable creators, formidable warriors, and guardians of lore brought from the West, they also bear the memory of their oaths, their faults, and the kingdoms they failed to preserve.

Apparence

Les Noldor sont les plus grands et les plus robustes des Elfes, tout en restant plus minces et plus gracieux que les Hommes. Les hommes atteignent fréquemment deux mètres, tandis que les femmes sont à peine moins grandes. Leur corps associe force, agilité et légèreté, sans la lourdeur physique des peuples mortels.

Leur mémoire est d’une précision extraordinaire. Ils peuvent se rappeler des lieux, des visages, des chants et des événements vieux de plusieurs millénaires avec une netteté presque immédiate. Cette faculté est à la fois un don et un fardeau : les joies anciennes restent présentes, mais les pertes, les fautes et les humiliations ne s’effacent jamais complètement.

Les Noldor ne dorment pas au sens humain. Ils se reposent par une méditation profonde durant laquelle ils revivent leurs souvenirs. Quelques heures leur suffisent généralement, et ils peuvent poursuivre leur route pendant plusieurs jours lorsqu’une nécessité impérieuse l’exige.

Ils voient sous la lumière des étoiles ou de la lune presque aussi clairement qu’en plein jour. Leur ouïe est également exceptionnelle, ce qui contribue à leur maîtrise de la musique, du chant et des langues.

Leurs pas sont extrêmement légers. Ils laissent peu de traces de leur passage et peuvent marcher sur une neige fraîche sans s’y enfoncer comme le feraient les Hommes. Les tentatives visant à les pister sont donc particulièrement difficiles.

Le peuple du savoir

Le mot Noldor est lié au savoir, à la connaissance profonde et à la recherche de compréhension. Ils ne se contentent pas d’observer le monde : ils veulent connaître ses principes, ses structures et les moyens de le transformer.

Leur curiosité peut cependant devenir une faiblesse. Un Noldo ne supporte pas facilement qu’une énigme demeure irrésolue ou qu’un domaine de savoir lui échappe. Cette volonté de comprendre et de créer nourrit leurs plus grandes œuvres, mais aussi plusieurs de leurs catastrophes.

Aucun Noldo n’incarne mieux leur grandeur et leurs dangers que Fëanor, créateur des Silmarils. Son génie, sa volonté et son talent dépassaient ceux de presque tous les autres Enfants d’Ilúvatar. Les Noldor ne considèrent pas la création comme un simple métier. Façonner une lame, une gemme, une cité ou un chant consiste à exprimer une part de soi dans le monde. L’œuvre devient alors intimement liée à son créateur, ce qui explique la douleur extrême provoquée par sa destruction, son vol ou sa profanation.

Durant le Premier Âge, les Noldor fondèrent plusieurs royaumes en Beleriand. Ces royaumes étaient à la fois des refuges, des centres de savoir et des remparts contre Morgoth. Ils furent presque tous détruits par la guerre, la trahison, l’orgueil ou la puissance de l’Ennemi.

La perte de Gondolin, de Nargothrond et des autres cités demeure inscrite dans la mémoire des survivants. Un Noldo des Âges ultérieurs peut avoir connu personnellement ces lieux ou avoir reçu le récit de leur chute de parents qui y vécurent.

Les Noldor sont passionnés, fiers, curieux et intensément déterminés. Ils ressentent profondément la joie, la colère, l’amour, l’humiliation et le désir de vengeance.

Ils voient sous la lumière des étoiles ou de la lune presque aussi clairement qu’en plein jour. Leur ouïe est également exceptionnelle, ce qui contribue à leur maîtrise de la musique, du chant et des langues.

Leurs pas sont extrêmement légers. Ils laissent peu de traces de leur passage et peuvent marcher sur une neige fraîche sans s’y enfoncer comme le feraient les Hommes. Les tentatives visant à les pister sont donc particulièrement difficiles.

Le peuple du savoir

Le mot Noldor est lié au savoir, à la connaissance profonde et à la recherche de compréhension. Ils ne se contentent pas d’observer le monde : ils veulent connaître ses principes, ses structures et les moyens de le transformer.

Leur curiosité peut cependant devenir une faiblesse. Un Noldo ne supporte pas facilement qu’une énigme demeure irrésolue ou qu’un domaine de savoir lui échappe. Cette volonté de comprendre et de créer nourrit leurs plus grandes œuvres, mais aussi plusieurs de leurs catastrophes.

Fëanor et l’art de créer

Aucun Noldo n’incarne mieux leur grandeur et leurs dangers que Fëanor, créateur des Silmarils. Son génie, sa volonté et son talent dépassaient ceux de presque tous les autres Enfants d’Ilúvatar. Pourtant, son orgueil, sa possessivité et son refus de renoncer à son œuvre entraînèrent les siens dans l’exil, le meurtre fratricide et une guerre sans espoir contre Morgoth.

Les Noldor ne considèrent pas la création comme un simple métier. Façonner une lame, une gemme, une cité ou un chant consiste à exprimer une part de soi dans le monde. L’œuvre devient alors intimement liée à son créateur, ce qui explique la douleur extrême provoquée par sa destruction, son vol ou sa profanation.

Royaumes de Beleriand

Durant le Premier Âge, les Noldor fondèrent plusieurs royaumes en Beleriand. Ces royaumes étaient à la fois des refuges, des centres de savoir et des remparts contre Morgoth. Ils furent presque tous détruits par la guerre, la trahison, l’orgueil ou la puissance de l’Ennemi.

La perte de Gondolin, de Nargothrond et des autres cités demeure inscrite dans la mémoire des survivants. Un Noldo des Âges ultérieurs peut avoir connu personnellement ces lieux ou avoir reçu le récit de leur chute de parents qui y vécurent.

Après la Guerre de la Colère

À la fin du Premier Âge, une grande partie des Noldor accepta le pardon des Valar et retourna vers l’Ouest. D’autres demeurèrent en Terre du Milieu, par attachement à leurs œuvres, par amour des terres qu’ils avaient défendues ou parce qu’ils n’étaient pas encore prêts à renoncer à leur rôle dans l’histoire du monde.

Durant le Deuxième Âge, certains s’établirent au Lindon sous l’autorité de Gil-galad. D’autres fondèrent l’Eregion, où les Gwaith-i-Mírdain travaillèrent avec les Nains de Khazad-dûm. C’est là que furent forgés les Anneaux de Pouvoir, œuvre splendide née d’un désir sincère de préserver la beauté de la Terre du Milieu, mais corrompue par les conseils de Sauron.

Après la destruction de l’Eregion, les principaux refuges noldorins furent le Lindon et Fondcombe. Leur population diminua progressivement à mesure que les survivants prenaient la mer vers Aman.

Tempérament

Les Noldor sont passionnés, fiers, curieux et intensément déterminés. Ils ressentent profondément la joie, la colère, l’amour, l’humiliation et le désir de vengeance.

Ils supportent difficilement l’échec, l’ignorance ou l’impuissance. Leur confiance en leurs capacités peut les conduire à sous-estimer les avertissements, à poursuivre un projet dangereux ou à croire qu’aucune limite ne saurait leur être imposée.

Leur orgueil n’est cependant pas toujours de l’arrogance. Il peut aussi prendre la forme d’une dignité inflexible, d’un refus de céder devant l’Ombre ou d’une volonté de réparer les fautes anciennes.

Serments et fidélité

Les Noldor donnent une grande force aux paroles prononcées. Un serment solennel engage l’identité même de celui qui le prête. Le rompre est une honte presque insupportable, mais le respecter aveuglément peut conduire à des actes terribles.

Les serments servent à unir une maison, sceller une alliance, promettre une vengeance, protéger une œuvre, défendre un royaume ou préserver un secret. L’histoire du serment de Fëanor demeure un avertissement contre les paroles impossibles à reprendre.

Religion

Les Noldor révèrent Eru et connaissent intimement la nature des Valar. Ils n’entretiennent pourtant pas de clergé formel. Leur foi s’exprime par le chant, la poésie, la méditation, la création artistique et la célébration des œuvres du monde.

Ils honorent particulièrement Varda, qu’ils nomment Elentári ou Elbereth, la Dame des Étoiles. Aulë occupe également une place importante en raison de son enseignement des arts de la matière, de la forge et de la création.

Leur relation avec les Valar reste complexe. Beaucoup éprouvent à leur égard amour et respect, mais aussi honte, défiance ou culpabilité en raison de l’exil des Noldor et des fautes du Premier Âge.

Langues

Le quenya est leur langue ancestrale, langue d’Aman, de la poésie savante, des chroniques et des cérémonies. Après leur retour en Terre du Milieu, ils adoptèrent largement le sindarin comme langue quotidienne.

Un Noldo instruit peut également connaître le telerin, le westron, très rarement le khuzdul, l’adûnaïque, diverses langues humaines et des langues anciennes ou occultes. Leur maîtrise linguistique est généralement exceptionnelle et ils accordent une grande importance à l’étymologie, aux noms et aux systèmes d’écriture.

Vêtements et apparat

Les Noldor apprécient les vêtements riches, élégants et parfaitement façonnés. Ils privilégient les étoffes fines, les couleurs profondes et les motifs liés aux étoiles, aux gemmes, aux arbres ou aux emblèmes de leur maison.

Le bleu profond, l’argent, le blanc, le noir, le rouge sombre, l’or et le vert intense sont fréquents. Leurs bijoux et ornements sont rarement excessifs : même les pièces les plus riches sont intégrées à une composition harmonieuse où chaque détail possède une fonction ou une signification.

Armes et armures

Les Noldor comptent parmi les meilleurs forgerons et guerriers des Peuples Libres. Ils utilisent épées longues, lances, arcs, haches, dagues, boucliers, mailles elfiques et armures finement ajustées.

Leurs lames peuvent porter des noms, des inscriptions et une histoire propre. Certaines furent forgées en Aman ou au Premier Âge et transmises durant des milliers d’années. Ils combattent avec rapidité, précision et discipline ; leur légèreté ne les empêche pas de porter des protections solides.

Magie

Les Noldor entretiennent une relation naturelle avec ce que les Hommes appellent la magie. Pour eux, il s’agit souvent d’une extension du savoir, de la volonté, du chant et de l’artisanat.

Leurs pratiques concernent l’enchantement des objets, les runes, la lumière, la protection, la perception, la connaissance, les éléments, la préservation des lieux et les chants de pouvoir. Les Noldor entretiennent une profonde parenté avec les Sindar, bien que leurs tempéraments et leurs histoires diffèrent. Ils respectent les Nains pour leur talent artisanal et leur connaissance de la pierre, mais leurs rivalités et leur orgueil peuvent provoquer des conflits.

Ils voient souvent les Hommes avec un mélange d’admiration, de compassion et de condescendance. Leur brièveté de vie les attriste, mais leur capacité à changer rapidement le monde les fascine.

La Culture noldorine favorise les combattants, bardes, magiciens, alchimistes, mystiques, érudits, artisans, forgerons, joailliers, architectes, capitaines et diplomates.

Leur formation comprend naturellement les langues, l’histoire, les runes, les arts, la perception, les armes, la magie, la forge, l’artisanat et la connaissance des peuples.

Place dans la création de personnage

La Culture Noldor convient particulièrement à un Elfe issu d’Aman ou de Tirion au Premier Âge, d’une maison noldorine de Beleriand, du Lindon, de l’Eregion, de Fondcombe ou d’une lignée ayant choisi de demeurer en Terre du Milieu.

Elle est disponible durant les quatre Âges, mais devient progressivement plus rare. Aux Troisième et Quatrième Âges, un Noldo est souvent un être ancien, membre d’une petite communauté ou héritier d’une lignée dont beaucoup ont déjà quitté la Terre du Milieu.

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

Fëanor and the art of creation

No Noldo better embodies both their greatness and their dangers than Fëanor, maker of the Silmarils. His genius, will, and skill surpassed those of nearly all the other Children of Ilúvatar. Yet his pride, possessiveness, and refusal to relinquish his work led his people into exile, kinslaying, and a hopeless war against Morgoth.

The Noldor do not regard creation as merely a trade. To shape a blade, a gem, a city, or a song is to express a part of oneself within the world. The work thus becomes intimately bound to its maker, which explains the extreme pain caused by its destruction, theft, or desecration.

Kingdoms of Beleriand

During the First Age, the Noldor founded several realms in Beleriand. These kingdoms were at once refuges, centres of learning, and bulwarks against Morgoth. Nearly all were destroyed by war, betrayal, pride, or the power of the Enemy.

The loss of Gondolin, Nargothrond, and the other cities remains engraved in the memory of the survivors. A Noldo of a later Age may personally have known these places, or may have received the tale of their fall from parents who lived there.

After the War of Wrath

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Others remained in Middle-earth, through attachment to their works, love for the lands they had defended, or because they were not yet ready to relinquish their role in the history of the world.

During the Second Age, some settled in Lindon under the authority of Gil-galad. Others founded Eregion, where the Gwaith-i-Mírdain worked alongside the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm. There the Rings of Power were forged, a splendid achievement born from a sincere desire to preserve the beauty of Middle-earth, but corrupted by the counsels of Sauron.

After the destruction of Eregion, the chief Noldorin refuges were Lindon and Rivendell. Their population gradually dwindled as the survivors took ship for Aman.

Temperament

The Noldor are passionate, proud, curious, and intensely determined. They feel joy, anger, love, humiliation, and the desire for vengeance with great depth.

They have difficulty enduring failure, ignorance, or helplessness. Confidence in their own abilities can lead them to disregard warnings, pursue dangerous projects, or believe that no limit should be imposed upon them.

Their pride is not always arrogance, however. It can also take the form of unyielding dignity, refusal to yield before the Shadow, or determination to repair ancient wrongs.

Oaths and loyalty

The Noldor invest spoken words with great force. A solemn oath binds the very identity of the one who swears it. To break it is an almost unbearable disgrace, yet to obey it blindly can lead to terrible deeds.

Oaths may unite a house, seal an alliance, promise vengeance, protect a work, defend a kingdom, or preserve a secret. The history of the Oath of Fëanor remains a warning against words that cannot be taken back.

Religion

The Noldor revere Eru and possess intimate knowledge of the nature of the Valar. Yet they maintain no formal clergy. Their faith is expressed through song, poetry, meditation, artistic creation, and celebration of the works of the world.

They especially honour Varda, whom they call Elentári or Elbereth, the Lady of the Stars. Aulë also holds an important place because of his teaching concerning matter, smithcraft, and creation.

Their relationship with the Valar remains complex. Many feel love and respect toward them, but also shame, distrust, or guilt because of the exile of the Noldor and the wrongs committed during the First Age.

Languages

Quenya is their ancestral language, the tongue of Aman, learned poetry, chronicles, and ceremony. After their return to Middle-earth, they widely adopted Sindarin as their everyday language.

An educated Noldo may also know Telerin, Westron, very rarely Khuzdul, Adûnaic, various Mannish tongues, and ancient or occult languages. Their linguistic mastery is generally exceptional, and they attach great importance to etymology, names, and systems of writing.

Clothing and display

The Noldor appreciate rich, elegant, perfectly crafted clothing. They favour fine fabrics, deep colours, and designs associated with stars, gems, trees, or the emblems of their house.

Deep blue, silver, white, black, dark red, gold, and intense green are common. Their jewellery and ornaments are rarely excessive: even the richest pieces are integrated into a harmonious composition in which every detail has a purpose or meaning.

Weapons and armour

The Noldor rank among the finest smiths and warriors of the Free Peoples. They use longswords, spears, bows, axes, daggers, shields, Elven mail, and finely fitted armour.

Their blades may bear names, inscriptions, and histories of their own. Some were forged in Aman or during the First Age and passed down for thousands of years. They fight with speed, precision, and discipline; their lightness does not prevent them from wearing solid protection.

Magic

The Noldor have a natural relationship with what Men call magic. To them, it is often an extension of knowledge, will, song, and craft.

Their practices concern the enchantment of objects, runes, light, protection, perception, knowledge, the elements, preservation of places, and songs of power. They produce more practitioners of Essence than other Elven cultures, without excluding Channeling or Mentalism.

Relations with other peoples

The Noldor share deep kinship with the Sindar, although their temperaments and histories differ. They respect Dwarves for their craftsmanship and knowledge of stone, but rivalry and pride can provoke conflict.

They often view Men with a mixture of admiration, compassion, and condescension. The brevity of human life saddens them, while humanity's ability to change the world quickly fascinates them.

They hate Morgoth, Sauron, Orcs, and creatures born of their corruption. This hatred is nourished by personal losses that even millennia are insufficient to erase.

Professions and training

Noldorin Culture favours warriors, bards, magicians, alchemists, mystics, scholars, craftsmen, smiths, jewellers, architects, captains, and diplomats.

Their training naturally includes languages, history, runes, the arts, perception, weapons, magic, smithcraft, crafts, and knowledge of peoples.

Place in character creation

Noldorin Culture is particularly appropriate for an Elf from Aman or Tirion in the First Age, a Noldorin house of Beleriand, Lindon, Eregion, Rivendell, or a lineage that chose to remain in Middle-earth.

It is available during all four Ages, but becomes progressively rarer. In the Third and Fourth Ages, a Noldo is often an ancient being, a member of a small community, or the heir of a lineage many of whose members have already left Middle-earth.

The Noldor embody both the grandeur and tragedy of the Eldar: incomparable creators, formidable warriors, and guardians of lore brought from the West, they also bear the memory of their oaths, their faults, and the kingdoms they failed to preserve.

The Noldor, sometimes called High Elves, Deep Elves, Golodhrim, Gelydh, or Nómin, are the second of the three great kindreds of the Eldar. They are descended from the Elves who undertook the Great Journey westward and dwelt in Aman beneath the light of the Two Trees. Among the Elves who still remain in Middle-earth, they alone have directly known the Blessed Realm and the teaching of the Valar. It is this experience, more than their rank or power, that earns them the name High Elves.

Their first king was Finwë. His sons — Fëanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin — gave rise to the three great historical branches of the Noldor. The oaths, rivalries, and tragedies bound to these houses shaped much of their history during the First Age.

Appearance

The Noldor are the tallest and most robust of the Elves, while still remaining slimmer and more graceful than Men. Males frequently reach two metres in height, while females are only slightly shorter. Their bodies combine strength, agility, and lightness without the physical heaviness of mortal peoples.

Most have black or very dark brown hair and grey eyes, often shining with remarkable intensity. Descendants of Fingolfin and Finarfin may, however, have fair or golden hair and blue eyes because of their Vanyarin ancestry.

Their features are fine and regular, and they are beardless. Their skin normally bears neither lasting scars nor marks of disease. Those who beheld the light of Aman sometimes seem surrounded by an inner radiance perceptible even to other Elves.

Immortality and memory

Like all Elves, the Noldor do not age in the same way as Men. Their bodies reach maturity and then remain almost unchanged. They normally die only through violence or when a profound weariness of the world deprives them of the will to live.

Their memory is extraordinarily precise. They can recall places, faces, songs, and events several millennia old with almost immediate clarity. This gift is both a blessing and a burden: ancient joys remain present, but losses, mistakes, and humiliations never completely fade.

The Noldor do not sleep in the human sense. They rest through deep meditation during which they relive their memories. A few hours generally suffice, and they can continue travelling for several days when urgent necessity requires it.

Endurance and senses

Their delicate appearance conceals considerable strength and endurance. They can walk or ride through very long days without showing obvious fatigue and withstand natural cold remarkably well.

They see beneath starlight or moonlight almost as clearly as in full day. Their hearing is likewise exceptional, contributing to their mastery of music, song, and languages.

Their steps are extraordinarily light. They leave few traces of their passage and can walk over fresh snow without sinking into it as Men would. Attempts to track them are therefore particularly difficult.

The people of knowledge

The word Noldor is associated with lore, deep knowledge, and the pursuit of understanding. They are not content merely to observe the world: they seek to know its principles, its structures, and the means by which it can be transformed.

Their curiosity can, however, become a weakness. A Noldo does not easily tolerate an unsolved riddle or a field of knowledge beyond his understanding. This desire to comprehend and create nourishes their greatest works, but also several of their catastrophes.

Fëanor and the art of creation

No Noldo better embodies both their greatness and their dangers than Fëanor, maker of the Silmarils. His genius, will, and skill surpassed those of nearly all the other Children of Ilúvatar. Yet his pride, possessiveness, and refusal to relinquish his work led his people into exile, kinslaying, and a hopeless war against Morgoth.

The Noldor do not regard creation as merely a trade. To shape a blade, a gem, a city, or a song is to express a part of oneself within the world. The work thus becomes intimately bound to its maker, which explains the extreme pain caused by its destruction, theft, or desecration.

During the First Age, the Noldor founded several realms in Beleriand. These kingdoms were at once refuges, centres of learning, and bulwarks against Morgoth. Nearly all were destroyed by war, betrayal, pride, or the power of the Enemy.

The loss of Gondolin, Nargothrond, and the other cities remains engraved in the memory of the survivors. A Noldo of a later Age may personally have known these places, or may have received the tale of their fall from parents who lived there.

After the War of Wrath

At the end of the First Age, a great part of the Noldor accepted the pardon of the Valar and returned westward. Others remained in Middle-earth, through attachment to their works, love for the lands they had defended, or because they were not yet ready to relinquish their role in the history of the world.

During the Second Age, some settled in Lindon under the authority of Gil-galad. Others founded Eregion, where the Gwaith-i-Mírdain worked alongside the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm. There the Rings of Power were forged, a splendid achievement born from a sincere desire to preserve the beauty of Middle-earth, but corrupted by the counsels of Sauron.

After the destruction of Eregion, the chief Noldorin refuges were Lindon and Rivendell. Their population gradually dwindled as the survivors took ship for Aman.

The Noldor are passionate, proud, curious, and intensely determined. They feel joy, anger, love, humiliation, and the desire for vengeance with great depth.

They have difficulty enduring failure, ignorance, or helplessness. Confidence in their own abilities can lead them to disregard warnings, pursue dangerous projects, or believe that no limit should be imposed upon them.

Their pride is not always arrogance, however. It can also take the form of unyielding dignity, refusal to yield before the Shadow, or determination to repair ancient wrongs.
